Where it began

Zaheer Abbas was born in Sialkot on 24 July 1947 and studied at Murray College. He was one of the very few top cricketers to play in spectacles, which never seemed to slow him down.

His first Test came in 1969. In only his second, at Edgbaston in 1971, he made 274 against England, batting for some nine hours. It answered any doubts about how he would cope with seam and swing, and it was the first of four double-centuries he made in Tests.

The player

He played 78 Tests for Pakistan between 1969 and 1985 and made 5,062 runs at 44.80, with 12 hundreds and 20 fifties. He also held 34 catches and captained his country in 14 Tests, of which three were won and only one lost. He was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year.

His 215 against India in 1983 was his hundredth first-class century, which put him alongside Geoffrey Boycott as the only men to reach that landmark during a Test. He was also the first Asian batsman to make a hundred first-class hundreds. In one-day cricket he was ahead of his time, scoring quickly and becoming, in 1982/1983, the first man to make three hundreds in a row in one-day internationals.

What made him special

Writers who watched him kept reaching for the same words: elegant, wristy, effortless. He had a high, flowing backlift, played very late and found the gaps on the off side with his cover drive. He was especially good against spin, and he scored his runs at a lively pace without ever seeming to hurry. People called him the Asian Bradman.

Like most batsmen before helmets, he was less fond of the short ball than of the half-volley. Few held it against him.

Away from the middle

He spent thirteen seasons at Gloucestershire from 1972, playing 206 first-class matches and making 49 hundreds. Twice, in 1976 and 1981, he passed two thousand runs in a season. Four times he made a hundred and a double-hundred in the same match, and he was not out in all eight of those innings.

After playing he served as a match referee and as manager of the national team, and in 2015 he became President of the ICC, only the third cricketer to hold the post. Pakistan gave him the Pride of Performance in 1971 and the Sitara-e-Imtiaz in 2018. He entered the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in 2020 and the PCB Hall of Fame in 2021. In 1983 he wrote his autobiography, Zed, with the journalist David Foot.

And finally

For a man who batted in glasses, he seemed to see the ball earlier than almost anyone. Bowlers in England spent thirteen summers wishing he had needed a stronger prescription.
